questions.q: Which of the following is NOT typically considered part of static testing?
questions.e: Statement coverage is measured by running the code, so it's dynamic. Inspections, walkthroughs and desk checks examine the code without running it.

questions.q: In a system with high cyclomatic complexity, what is the best justification for applying condition coverage instead of relying solely on statement coverage?
o: Statement coverage alone always achieves 100% functional validation
Condition coverage is simpler and faster to implement
Statement coverage can miss logical errors in compound Boolean expressions
Cyclomatic complexity only affects black-box test cases
questions.e: Statement coverage can execute an `if (a || b)` line without ever testing each condition as true and false, so faults in compound conditions slip through.

questions.q: The cost of fixing a fault:
o: Is more expensive if found in requirements than functional design.
Decreases as we move the product towards production.
Increases as we move the product towards production.
questions.e: The later a defect is found, the more work has been built on it, so the cost of fixing it rises the closer the product gets to production.

questions.q: Why is desk checking considered a limited form of static testing?
o: It lacks structured review and may miss subtle defects
questions.e: Desk checking is one person reading their own code, with no structured process or second pair of eyes, so subtle defects get missed.

questions.q: In JUnit, what happens when an assertion fails?
o: The test is marked as failed
questions.e: A failed assertion throws an AssertionError; JUnit records that test as failed and carries on with the others.

questions.q: Which metric indicates how many defects are found during testing versus those found by users post-release?
questions.e: Defect detection efficiency (DDE) = defects found in testing ÷ (defects found in testing + defects found after release).

questions.q: Consider a test case designed using Equivalence Partitioning for a shipping system charging $5 for weights 0–1 kg, $3/kg for 1.01–5 kg, $2/kg for 5.01–15 kg, and $1/kg for >15 kg. Which of the following test inputs would best validate a boundary condition defect missed by typical partitioning?
o: 5.00 kg and 5.01 kg in a single comparative test
questions.e: A boundary defect sits exactly where one rate switches to the next. Testing 5.00 and 5.01 together checks both sides of that boundary, which a single value from each partition can miss. (This key is our answer: on the marked paper, 5.0 kg alone was marked wrong.)

questions.q: Why is test case prioritization important in regression testing?
o: It reduces cost and time by focusing on the most critical tests first
questions.e: Regression suites grow large; prioritizing runs the most important or riskiest tests first, so major problems are found early when time is short.

questions.q: Why is test coverage (e.g., requirement coverage and code coverage) considered a key quality metric in software testing? Discuss how it influences test planning.
questions.m: Coverage measures how much of the system the tests actually exercise: requirement coverage = requirements covered by tests ÷ total requirements × 100, code coverage = statements/branches executed ÷ total × 100. It's a key quality metric because untested requirements and code are where defects hide, so low coverage means high risk and little confidence. In planning it shows exactly where the gaps are: the team adds tests for uncovered requirements and code, prioritizes the riskiest gaps, and uses coverage targets as exit criteria (you can't control what you can't measure).

questions.q: In integration testing, explain the difference between top-down and bottom-up approaches. When would you prefer each strategy?
questions.m: Top-down integration starts with the top-level control module and adds the modules below it one level at a time, using stubs to stand in for lower modules that aren't ready. Bottom-up starts with the lowest-level modules, tests them together in clusters and works upward, using drivers to call them. Prefer top-down when you want an early working skeleton of the system and to check the main control flow and design early. Prefer bottom-up when the low-level modules (utilities, hardware or data access) are critical, complex or finished first, since faults there are found early and no stubs are needed.

questions.q: What role does a test oracle play in software testing? Provide an example where a poorly defined oracle can lead to incorrect test results.
questions.m: A test oracle is the source that tells you the expected result of a test (a spec, a previous version, a calculation, a human expert). The tester compares the actual result with it to decide pass or fail. If the oracle is poorly defined the verdict is unreliable. Example: the requirement says the search must be “fast”. One tester passes a 4-second response, another fails it, so the same behaviour gets different verdicts, and a real performance defect can pass (a false pass). An oracle built from an outdated spec can also fail correct behaviour (a false failure).

questions.q: Explain how test metrics like “defect density” and “test case effectiveness” can guide decision-making in the final stages of a software release.
questions.m: Defect density (defects ÷ size, e.g. per KLOC or per module) shows how buggy the product or each component still is, and which modules are hot spots. Test case effectiveness (defects found by tests ÷ total defects, or defects found per test) shows whether the tests are actually catching defects. Near release they drive the go/no-go decision: high density or low effectiveness means the product isn't ready, so add or improve tests on the weak modules, fix the defects or delay the release; low density with high effectiveness gives confidence to release.

questions.q: Static Testing can help in checking several things, give 4 things can be tested in static testing.
questions.m: Any four of: requirements and design documents (ambiguities, omissions, inconsistencies); deviations from coding standards; syntax and logic errors; unreachable (dead) code and unused or undefined variables; interface mismatches; security vulnerabilities; maintainability and code complexity; test plans and test cases themselves.

questions.q: Write down one or more test cases, such that this/these test case(s) together satisfy Decision coverage. State clearly which parts of the test(s) cover which part of the code.
questions.m: Six decisions need a true and a false outcome each: D1 the length check, D2 the for loop, D3 A[i] > B[i], D4 A[i] > C[i], D5 A[i] == C[i], D6 B[i] > C[i]. TestABCCovers T1{1}{1, 2}{1}D1 true (lengths differ, prints “not of equal length”) T2{3, 2, 2, 1, 1}{1, 1, 1, 3, 2}{1, 2, 3, 2, 3}D1 false; D2 true five times then false. i=0: D3 T, D4 T (A largest). i=1: D3 T, D4 F, D5 T (A equals C). i=2: D3 T, D4 F, D5 F (C largest). i=3: D3 F, D6 T (B largest). i=4: D3 F, D6 F (C largest or equal to B) Two tests give 100% decision coverage. Splitting T2 into five one-element tests is just as correct; what matters is that every decision is shown both true and false and you say which test covers which outcome.

questions.q: Calculate the cyclomatic complexity.
questions.m: V(G) = number of decisions + 1. The decisions are the length check, the for loop, A[i] > B[i], A[i] > C[i], A[i] == C[i] and B[i] > C[i]: 6 decisions, so V(G) = 6 + 1 = 7. If you count each condition of the compound || as its own predicate node, you get 7 + 1 = 8, which is also accepted. (The marked paper gave full marks for 5 + 1 = 6, which leaves out the for loop.)

questions.q: B. You are testing a mobile data plan billing system based on monthly data usage. The billing rules are: the first 2 GB are included in the monthly base plan and cost nothing extra; the next 3 GB (up to 5 GB) are charged at $2 per GB; the next 5 GB (up to 10 GB) are charged at $1.5 per GB; any usage above 10 GB is charged at $1 per GB. Using the Equivalence Partitioning technique, identify the different equivalence classes for the data usage field and provide at least one test case for each class.
questions.m: Classes for usage U (GB), one test value from inside each: invalid U < 0 → −1 (rejected); valid 1 0 ≤ U ≤ 2 → 1 GB, $0 extra; valid 2 2 < U ≤ 5 → 3.5 GB, 1.5 × $2 = $3; valid 3 5 < U ≤ 10 → 7 GB, $6 + 2 × $1.5 = $9; valid 4 U > 10 → 15 GB, $6 + $7.5 + 5 × $1 = $18.5. Decide which class 2, 5 and 10 GB themselves fall in (the marker asked “what about = 10?”) and say so.

questions.q: C. You are testing the Online Loan Application System for a financial institution. The system validates: (1) Applicant Age between 21 and 65 years inclusive; (2) Annual Income at least $15,000 USD; (3) Requested Loan Amount between $5,000 and $500,000, and not more than 10× the applicant’s annual income; (4) Credit Score 600 or higher. Using Boundary Value Analysis, identify the key boundary values for each of the four input fields, and design a minimum of 2 test cases per field.
questions.m: Test just below, on and just above each boundary. Age: 20 (reject), 21 (accept), 65 (accept), 66 (reject). Income: 14,999 (reject), 15,000 (accept). Loan amount: 4,999 (reject), 5,000 (accept), 500,000 (accept), 500,001 (reject); and against income, with income $20,000: loan 200,000 = 10× (accept) and 200,001 (reject). Credit score: 599 (reject), 600 (accept). Note the boundaries themselves (21, 65, 15,000, 5,000, 500,000, 600) are valid; the marked paper lost marks for testing only 20/66 and 22/64.

questions.q: Using the data above, calculate the following metrics.
questions.m: a. Requirements coverage = validated ÷ total requirements × 100 = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. b. Defect density per test hour = defects found ÷ hours = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 defects/hour (the only hours given are the 10 hours; the marked paper accepted this). c. MTTR = repair hours ÷ defects fixed = 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes. d. Fixed defects % = fixed ÷ defects reported × 100 = 40 ÷ 50 = 80% (the marked paper lost marks for dividing by the 150 test cases). e. Test effectiveness = defects found in testing ÷ (found in testing + found post-release) × 100 = 50 ÷ (50 + 150) = 25%.

questions.q: Interpret your results: for each metric calculated, briefly explain what the value implies about the software quality, testing efficiency, or release readiness of the system.
questions.m: Requirements coverage 25%: three quarters of the requirements were never validated, so most of the system is untested and risky. 5 defects per hour: the product is defect-heavy. MTTR 15 minutes: once found, defects are fixed quickly, so the fixing process is efficient. 80% fixed: 10 known defects (some possibly critical) were released unfixed. Test effectiveness 25%: customers found three times as many defects as testing did, so the testing was ineffective. Overall the system was not ready for release: widen coverage and improve the tests before the next release.

questions.q: List three types of data that need to be tested for performance testing, then discuss the importance of using appropriate test data in performance testing.
questions.m: Three kinds of test data: (1) volume data, i.e. production-sized databases and large files; (2) load data, i.e. realistic numbers of concurrent users, sessions and transactions; (3) peak or stress data, beyond the expected maximum and with varied, realistic input mixes, while measuring response time and throughput. Appropriate data matters because performance depends on the data: a small or unrealistic data set makes the system look fast and hides bottlenecks (slow queries, memory leaks, locking), so the results would be misleading. Production-like data gives results you can trust when deciding whether the system will cope in real use.

questions.q: Total Cost of Quality (CoQ) includes
o: Cost of Conformance (CoC) + Cost of Non-Conformance (CoNC)
Cost of Conformance (CoC) + Cost of Non-Conformance (CoNC) + Manual efforts
questions.e: CoQ = cost of conformance (prevention + appraisal) + cost of non-conformance (internal + external failures).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT included in the Cost of Non-Conformance?
questions.e: Quality planning is prevention, which is a cost of conformance. Failures and rework are the cost of non-conformance.

questions.q: Is a test that is performed at the development organization site.
questions.e: Alpha testing happens at the developer's site; beta testing happens at the customers' sites.

questions.q: Which of the following defines “Average amount of time a system operates before it fails”?
questions.e: MTTF is the average operating time before a failure. MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, and MTTR is the average repair time.

questions.q: Which of the following defines “The probability of a system to operate without failures”?
questions.e: Reliability is the probability of failure-free operation over a period. Availability is the share of time the system is up.

questions.q: Deviation of the observed behavior of a system from its specification, i.e., its expected behavior is called
questions.e: A failure is the visible deviation from expected behaviour. An error (mistake) by a person causes a defect (fault) in the code, which may cause a failure when executed.

questions.q: Which of the following defines “software validation”?
o: Are we building the software right?
Are we building the right software?
questions.e: Validation: are we building the right product (does it meet the user's needs)? Verification: are we building the product right (does it meet the spec)?

questions.q: Which of the following is CORRECT about the term “test oracle”?
o: The expected outputs of software for given input
questions.e: An oracle supplies the expected output, the expected result is part of every test case, and automating the oracle is one of the hardest problems in test automation.

questions.q: If the cyclomatic complexity value of a code/program is more than 40, what can be said about the code/program?
o: It is well-written code and testability is high
It is moderately complicated and testability is medium
It is extremely complicated and not testable
It is very complicated and testability is low
questions.e: From the white-box slides: 1–10 well-written, high testability; 10–20 moderately complex, medium; 20–40 very complex, low testability; above 40 not testable. (The answer sheet photo appears to show D, but D is the 20–40 band.)

questions.q: Which of the following should be noted for each test level?
questions.e: Each test level is described by its generic objectives, test basis, test objects, typical defects and responsibilities.

questions.q: Which of the following testing types includes functional and non-functional testing?
questions.e: Component testing can cover both functional and non-functional characteristics (e.g. memory leaks, robustness). Stress testing is only non-functional; smoke testing is a quick functional check. This follows the answer sheet.

questions.q: Which of the following “is a way of testing software products (including code) and can be performed well before dynamic test execution”?
questions.e: Reviews are static testing: they examine work products without running them, so they can start long before execution.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a very formal review?
questions.e: Inspection is the most formal review: trained moderator, defined roles, entry/exit criteria and metrics.

questions.q: Which of the following roles has the chief responsibility for the documents to be reviewed and for the rework to be done during the reviews?
questions.e: The author wrote the work product and fixes the defects found in it.

questions.q: Software testing is NOT required to be a systematic process to identify the correctness, completeness, and quality of developed software.
questions.e: Testing must be systematic: planned, designed and controlled.

questions.q: With reference to the V-model, for every development activity there is a corresponding testing activity.
questions.e: That's the core V-model principle: each development phase has a matching test level.

questions.q: Test levels can be combined or reorganized depending on the nature of the project or the system architecture.
questions.e: Test levels are a model; projects merge or reorganize them to fit the context.

questions.q: Static and dynamic testing have the same objective.
questions.e: Both aim to find defects as early as possible and assess quality; they differ in how (without vs with executing the code).

questions.q: Static analysis can identify both the defects and failures.
questions.e: Static analysis finds defects directly in the code; failures only appear when the code runs (dynamic testing).

questions.q: Testing reduces the probability of undiscovered defects remaining in the software but even if no defects are found, it is not a proof of their absence.
questions.e: Principle 1: testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence.
